How to read the numbers on this site

Every temperature, time, and dimension here is a starting point taken from widely used ranges and manufacturer guidance, with sources linked. The filament maker's label and your printer's own profile come first. Test on a small part, change one thing at a time, and write down what worked.

Fleet notes last checked October 31, 2026. Beginner pages, print files, and JSON catalogs were checked November 7, 2026. Private lab tools stay on my personal dashboard and aren't part of this public site. Print-ready files are on Recent prints. Dashboards can fetch data/index.json.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Short definitions for this site. If a slicer uses a different word, it is usually the same idea.

The same list is data/glossary.json, in alphabetical order of the term you see here.

docs.title: 3MF
docs.text: A model or project file that can include plates, colors, and slicer settings. A Bambu 3MF may not print correctly on another brand until you re-slice it.

docs.title: ABS
docs.text: A strong filament that warps unless the air around it stays warm. It gives off styrene. Print it enclosed and ventilated.

docs.title: AMS / CFS / MMU
docs.text: Filament changers. One nozzle, several spools, and a purge each time the color changes. Bambu AMS, Creality CFS, and Prusa MMU3 are examples. Slot counts differ by model.

docs.title: ASA
docs.text: Like ABS, but it holds up better in sunlight. Same need for an enclosure and the same fume caution.

docs.title: Bed leveling
docs.text: Making the nozzle the same height above the plate everywhere it prints. Mesh leveling measures a grid of points and bends the path to follow a slightly warped bed.

docs.title: Bedslinger
docs.text: A printer whose bed slides in Y while the nozzle moves in X and Z. The moving bed can wobble tall prints. The Bambu A1 series is this general layout; their spec pages say open-frame rather than the word bedslinger.

docs.title: Bowden
docs.text: The extruder motor is away from the nozzle and feeds filament through a PTFE tube. Lighter head, fussier with soft filament.

docs.title: Bridge
docs.text: A horizontal span between two already-printed points. The slicer usually slows down and adds cooling so the strand can hang.

docs.title: Brim
docs.text: Extra loops of plastic stuck to the first layer, around the part, to keep corners down. You peel it off afterward.

docs.title: Build plate
docs.text: The flat surface the part sticks to. Often a spring-steel sheet with a PEI coating, clipped or magneted to the heated bed.

docs.title: Cartesian
docs.text: Motion along three straight axes. Prusa labels the MK4S Cartesian. People also use the word for bedslingers.

docs.title: Clog
docs.text: A blockage in the nozzle or hotend. The extruder clicks, and the print goes hollow. Heat creep, debris, or a nozzle too close to the plate are common causes.

docs.title: Cold pull
docs.text: A way to yank debris out of a nozzle: heat, feed a bit of filament, cool partway, and pull. The exact temperatures depend on the hotend. Use your printer's guide.

docs.title: CoreXY
docs.text: A motion style where the bed usually moves only in Z and two belts move the head in X and Y. Common on faster enclosed machines.

docs.title: Desiccant
docs.text: The drying beads in a spool box or AMS. They fill up. Recharge or replace them when the humidity card says so.

docs.title: Direct drive
docs.text: The extruder motor is on the toolhead, close to the nozzle. Better for flexible filament. A bit more moving weight.

docs.title: Elephant's foot
docs.text: The bottom layers bulge outward. The nozzle was too close, or the bed was hot enough to keep those layers soft.

docs.title: Enclosure
docs.text: Walls and a lid around the print. They hold heat and block drafts, which ABS and nylon need, and they keep fingers off a moving head.

docs.title: Extruder
docs.text: The gears that push filament into the hotend. Direct drive sits on the moving head. A Bowden extruder sits back on the frame and pushes through a tube.

docs.title: FDM / FFF
docs.text: Fused deposition modeling, also called fused filament fabrication. A printer melts plastic filament and draws the part one layer at a time.

docs.title: Filament
docs.text: The plastic strand the printer melts. Almost all desktop FDM machines use 1.75 mm filament.

docs.title: First layer
docs.text: The first pass of plastic on the plate. If this layer is even and stuck, most other problems get easier.

docs.title: Flow rate
docs.text: How much plastic the slicer asks for, as a percentage of the calculated amount. Also called extrusion multiplier. Tune it after temperature, not before.

docs.title: G-code
docs.text: The line-by-line instructions the printer follows: move here, heat this, extrude that. You rarely write it by hand.

docs.title: Gyroid
docs.text: A wavy infill pattern that is strong in more than one direction and prints without crossing itself. A good default when you do not want to think about it.

docs.title: Hardened nozzle
docs.text: A steel or harder tip that survives carbon-fiber and glass-fiber filament. Plain brass wears out quickly on those.

docs.title: Heat creep
docs.text: Heat traveling too far up the hotend so filament softens and jams before the melt zone. Classic PLA failure inside a hot closed box.

docs.title: Heated chamber
docs.text: An enclosure with its own heater, not just leftover heat from the bed. The spec that matters is the maximum chamber temperature, often 55–65 °C on current machines that publish one.

docs.title: Hotend
docs.text: The heated block, heat break, and nozzle that melt the filament. The nozzle temperature you set is the hotend temperature.

docs.title: Hygroscopic
docs.text: Absorbs water from the air. Wet PETG, TPU, and nylon pop, string, and print weak. Dry them.

docs.title: IDEX
docs.text: Independent dual extruders. Two heads that can print two materials, or copy and mirror a part. The Snapmaker J1s is an IDEX machine.

docs.title: Infill
docs.text: The lattice inside the part. 15% is plenty for many decorative prints. Functional parts often want more walls before they want more infill.

docs.title: Input shaping
docs.text: A motion calibration that cancels vibration so high speed does not leave ripples (ringing) on the walls.

docs.title: Ironing
docs.text: A second slow pass of the nozzle on the top surface to smooth it. It adds time and can scar the top if the flow is off.

docs.title: Layer height
docs.text: How thick each slice is. 0.20 mm is a common everyday height with a 0.4 mm nozzle. Thinner looks smoother and takes longer.

docs.title: Layer shift
docs.text: A whole layer (or the rest of the print) steps sideways. The nozzle usually hit something, or a belt skipped.

docs.title: Live Z
docs.text: Adjusting the nozzle height while the first layer is printing. Prusa's name for a Z-offset tweak you can do in real time.

docs.title: Nozzle
docs.text: The small metal tip the melted plastic leaves through. 0.4 mm is the usual size. Smaller nozzles show more detail and clog more easily.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text: Which way the part sits on the plate. It changes strength, supports, and the look of the layers. Layers are weakest between each other.

docs.title: Overhang
docs.text: A slope or underside with nothing under it. Gentle slopes print in mid-air. Steep ones need support or a smarter orientation.

docs.title: PEI
docs.text: A plastic coating on many build plates. Textured PEI grips PLA well. Smooth PEI can grip PETG so hard that you want glue as a release layer.

docs.title: Perimeter / wall
docs.text: The outlines of each layer. More walls make a part stronger faster than adding infill.

docs.title: PETG
docs.text: Tougher and a bit more heat-tolerant than PLA, and more likely to string. It can stick too well to smooth PEI.

docs.title: PID tuning
docs.text: A calibration so the hotend or bed holds a steady temperature instead of swinging. Most modern printers do this themselves.

docs.title: PLA
docs.text: The easy filament. Stiff, detailed, and happy with lots of cooling. It softens in a hot car. See Materials 101.

docs.title: Pressure advance
docs.text: A calibration that starts and stops extrusion pressure so corners are not blobby. Bambu calls a related feature flow dynamics. PrusaSlicer calls it linear advance.

docs.title: Prime tower / purge
docs.text: Extra plastic printed beside the part so a filament change or a second nozzle starts clean. Single-nozzle color changes waste more than a tool changer.

docs.title: PTFE tube
docs.text: The slippery white tube filament slides through. The ends wear out and cause clicks or under-extrusion. Cut replacements square.

docs.title: Raft
docs.text: A thick disposable platform printed under the whole part. Use it when the part itself will not stick. A brim is usually enough and wastes less plastic.

docs.title: Resin printing
docs.text: A printer that cures liquid resin with light, usually layer by layer in a vat (SLA or MSLA). Finer detail than FDM, and a different safety routine: gloves, washing, and curing.

docs.title: Retraction
docs.text: A short pull-back of filament before a travel move, so the nozzle does not dribble a string.

docs.title: Ringing / ghosting
docs.text: Ripples on the walls after a corner. Speed, acceleration, or a loose belt. Input shaping is the usual fix on printers that have it.

docs.title: Seam
docs.text: The little mark where each layer's outline starts and stops. You can hide it on a corner. You cannot delete it.

docs.title: Shell
docs.text: The solid outside of the part: walls plus top and bottom layers. The shell is what you see and what takes most of the load.

docs.title: Shore hardness
docs.text: How soft a flexible filament is. Shore A and Shore D are different scales. Compare the number only within the same scale, on the spool's data sheet.

docs.title: Skirt
docs.text: A loop printed around the part that does not touch it. It primes the nozzle so the real print does not start with an empty line.

docs.title: Slicer
docs.text: The program that turns a 3D model into layer instructions (G-code or a printer project). Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer, and Creality Print are common ones.

docs.title: Spaghetti
docs.text: A bird's nest of filament because the part came off the plate or a layer printed in the air. Stop the print. The nozzle is fine; the part is not.

docs.title: Spool
docs.text: The reel the filament is wound on. Cardboard and plastic spools both work, but some multi-material units dislike warped cardboard.

docs.title: Stepper motor
docs.text: The motor that moves an axis in small counted steps. If it skips, you get a layer shift or a missed step you can sometimes hear as a thud.

docs.title: STL
docs.text: A model file that is only the shape. No color, no plates, no printer settings.

docs.title: Stringing
docs.text: Fine hairs of plastic between parts. Often wet filament or a nozzle that is too hot, not a broken printer.

docs.title: Support
docs.text: Sacrificial plastic that holds up overhangs. It leaves marks. A second material that does not stick to the part makes removal much easier.

docs.title: Thermal runaway protection
docs.text: Firmware that shuts the heater off if the temperature does not rise as expected. Leave it on. It is a fire safeguard.

docs.title: Tolerance
docs.text: How much bigger a hole or gap needs to be so two printed parts fit. A 0.2 mm gap per side is a common starting point for a snug fit. Test it.

docs.title: Tool changer
docs.text: The printer swaps whole toolheads or hotends instead of purging one nozzle. Less wasted plastic, more moving parts. Snapmaker U1 and Flashforge Creator 5 Pro ship with four toolheads.

docs.title: TPU
docs.text: Flexible filament. Print it slower. Soft grades often cannot go through a filament changer.

docs.title: Under-extrusion
docs.text: Not enough plastic comes out. Walls look thin, gappy, or weak. Causes include a partial clog, printing too fast, or a tangled spool.

docs.title: VOC
docs.text: Volatile organic compounds, gases released when plastic is hot. ABS and nylon are the ones to take seriously. See Safety.

docs.title: Volumetric flow
docs.text: How many cubic millimeters of plastic the hotend can melt per second. Printing faster than that limit causes under-extrusion no matter what the speed slider says.

docs.title: Warping
docs.text: Corners lifting off the plate as the plastic cools and shrinks. Common with ABS, ASA, nylon, and PC. An enclosure and a brim help.

docs.title: Z-banding
docs.text: Repeating horizontal ridges up the walls. Often a mechanical Z-axis problem, not a filament setting.

docs.title: Z-offset
docs.text: How far the nozzle sits from the plate on the first layer. Too high and lines do not stick. Too low and they squash into elephant's foot or grind the plate.

docs.title: What to buy
docs.text:
Buy the smallest machine that fits the parts you will print this month, in the material you will actually use. PLA on a simple printer teaches you more than a flagship that sits in the box.

The dated spec table is Printer comparison. This page is how to read it. Numbers below that name a price are the from-prices or sale prices we copied on 2026-11-07. They will change. Confirm them on the maker's site.

docs.title: Printer types
docs.text:
Open-frame, bed moves. The Bambu US store calls the A1 series open-frame. The bed or the gantry slides toward you. They are the usual first printer: easy to see, easy to fix, and a poor home for ABS. Tall thin parts can wobble because the bed is moving.

CoreXY. The bed usually only moves up and down. Two belts share the X and Y motion. Creality's K1C page, Elegoo's Centauri Carbon page, Anycubic's Kobra S1 page, Flashforge's AD5X page, and Prusa's CORE One+ page all say CoreXY. Many of these are enclosed. The motion type is not a quality score.

Enclosed. Walls and a door. They hold heat, which ABS, ASA, nylon, and polycarbonate want, and they keep hands off a fast head. PLA often wants the door open so the box does not get hot enough to jam. "Enclosed" on a spec sheet is not the same thing as a heated chamber.

Heated chamber. The box has its own heater and a published maximum, often 55–65 °C on the machines that state one. That is what you want for large nylon or PC parts. Leftover heat from the bed is weaker and usually unstated. If our table shows a dash, the page we read did not give a number.

Multi-color: filament changer. One nozzle, several spools. Bambu's store describes AMS and AMS Lite combos. Creality Hi uses CFS (4 spools, up to 16). Flashforge AD5X has a 4-color IFS built in. Every color change purges plastic into a wipe tower or a chute. It is slower and messier than the photos suggest, and soft TPU is often not allowed.

Tool changer. The printer parks extra toolheads and picks one up. Snapmaker U1 and Flashforge Creator 5 Pro ship with four. Bambu's H3C spec page says SwapTek 9-tool switching. Less purge, more mechanics, more money.

IDEX. Two independent heads. Snapmaker J1s can print two materials or copy and mirror a part. The bed gets narrower in copy mode. The spec page lists the smaller volumes.

Resin, briefly. A vat of liquid, a screen, and UV light. Beautiful miniatures. Not a first printer: nitrile gloves, isopropyl wash, a cure station, and a ventilated corner. Buy one later if you already like the process. None of the rows in the comparison table are resin machines.

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Build volume in millimeters, larger than your part. A 180 mm cube (A1 mini) is a lot of useful objects. A 350 mm cube (K2 Plus) is a different piece of furniture.
  • Nozzle temperature. 300 °C covers PLA, PETG, ABS, and many nylons. 350 °C shows up on the H2 series and the K2 Plus. Only chase it if you have a filament that asks for it.
  • Enclosure and a chamber number, if you want ABS or nylon. "Enclosed" without a chamber temperature still blocks drafts. It may not hold 60 °C.
  • Who changes the filament. Built-in (AD5X), optional and extra (AMS, CFS, MMU3), or several toolheads. Count the slots on the product page. Our table leaves a dash when the page did not say.
  • A hardened nozzle if the marketing mentions carbon fiber. Brass wears out on those filaments.
  • A parts story. Prusa sells kits and spare parts and documents the MK4S and CORE One+ in public. Closed machines are fine until a $40 fan is out of stock. Check that before you depend on it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Buying a multi-color flagship as a first printer, then fighting purges before you have printed a clean cube.
  • Trusting "500 mm/s" or "1000 mm/s" as the speed of a nice-looking part. Several makers also publish a lower "typical" or "print" speed. The table's speed note says which number we copied.
  • Assuming every enclosed printer can print ABS. Read the filament list. The A1 spec pages say ABS is not recommended.
  • Ignoring the room. ABS and nylon need ventilation. See Safety. A closed bedroom is a bad print farm.
  • Skipping the plate wash and then returning a printer that was fine.
  • Buying last year's model from a marketplace because a blog still calls it current. The X1 Carbon was not on Bambu's US collection page on 2026-11-07. The table leaves its price empty on purpose.

The lab's own six machines, with the mods on them, are a different page: Fleet. Use that when you are printing here. Use the comparison when you are shopping.

docs.title: Printer comparison
docs.text:
Specs were copied from manufacturer pages in late 2026. The date on each row is last_checked. A dash is not zero. It means that page did not state the value, or two sentences on the same page disagreed.

Best for and skill are our judgment from those specs. They are not a review score.

The machine-readable copy, including every note, is data/printers.json. How to read a row before you spend money is What to buy.

These four short lists are judgments from the specs below, not a lab test and not the manufacturer's ranking.

  • Best for beginners

    Bambu Lab A1 mini, Bambu Lab A1, Flashforge AD5X. Open machines with a low from-price, or a multicolor printer that already includes the color unit.

  • Best for multicolor

    Flashforge AD5X, Creality Hi, Snapmaker U1, Bambu Lab H2C. A built-in color system, a filament changer, or several toolheads.

  • Best for engineering filament

    Bambu Lab H2S, Bambu Lab X2D, Creality K2 Plus, Prusa CORE One+. A published heated chamber, or a high nozzle temperature on an enclosed machine.

  • Best for big prints

    Creality K2 Plus, Bambu Lab H2S, Bambu Lab H3C. The largest build volumes in this table.

docs.title: Choose
docs.text:
Before you slice anything, settle three things:

  1. The model: where it came from and what its license allows. See Model sources & licenses.
  2. The printer: which machine in the fleet suits the size, material, and color count. See Printer selector and the Fleet comparison.
  3. The material: what the part has to survive (heat, UV, impact, flex). See the Material matrix.

docs.title: Where to find models
docs.text:
Source Good for Notes Printables Functional parts, well-documented remixes Run by Prusa. Many models include print settings and "makes" photos. MakerWorld Ready-to-print 3MF projects, multicolor Run by Bambu Lab. 3MF projects carry plate and filament setup, so re-slice for non-Bambu printers. Thingiverse Large legacy library Older uploads vary a lot in quality. Check the comments and makes before printing. Manufacturer / CAD sites Exact-fit parts (brackets, mounts) Prefer official STEP files when you'll be modifying the part. Converters (e.g. BrickForge, from my guide library) Brick-compatible parts and MOCs Capabilities as described by the tool; not independently verified. Check fit and tolerances on a small test first.

3MF vs STL vs OBJ

STL is geometry only. 3MF can carry plates, colors, modifiers, and slicer settings. OBJ can carry color through a companion MTL file, so keep them together when importing. (From my OBJ vs. STL in Bambu Studio guide; import behavior varies by slicer version.)

docs.title: Printer selector
docs.text:
A quick "which machine?" guide for my fleet. Full specs and caveats are in the Fleet comparison.

If the job is… First choice Also works Why Largest single part or big batch (> 270 mm) Creality K2 Plus — 350 mm³ build volume, the only machine above ~270 mm Tall PLA/PETG part (up to 300 mm Z) Creality Hi K2 Plus 300 mm Z, open frame suits low-temp materials ABS / ASA / PC / PA, warp-prone K2 Plus or Creator 5 Pro X2D, X1C (Panda Breath) Actively heated chambers (60–65 °C per maker specs) Support-heavy part, clean underside Bambu X2D Creator 5 Pro, U1 Dual nozzle: dedicated support / interface material with little purge 4-color or 4-material job, low waste Snapmaker U1 or Creator 5 Pro — Independent toolheads, so no full filament purge per swap Many colors (> 4) X1C (AMS units) or K2 Plus (2 × CFS) — More slots, but each swap purges. Plan purge. Abrasive CF/GF filaments Printer with a hardened nozzle installed — Check nozzle first. U1 stock hotends are stainless steel, so check the abrasive guidance. TPU / flexible Creator 5 Pro (TPU listed by maker) or X1C via external spool — Most feeders/AMS units aren't approved for soft TPU. Check per-filament compatibility. Quick PLA prototype Whatever's free — Every machine handles PLA

Decision order

Size → material/heat → number of materials → nozzle (abrasive?) → availability.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text: This site is a Git repo. Every page is a Markdown file in docs/. Friends can suggest fixes the same way open-source docs work, through a pull request (PR).

docs.title: The quick way (no install)
docs.text:
1. Open the page on the site and click the ✏️ edit icon at the top right.
  2. GitHub opens the Markdown file. Make your change and describe it.
  3. Choose "Create a new branch and start a pull request".
  4. I'll review and merge. The site rebuilds automatically through GitHub Actions.

New to PRs? See GitHub Docs: Creating a pull request.

docs.title: What makes a good contribution
docs.text:
• Cite a source for every number (manufacturer wiki, data sheet, Prusa KB, or "my test, printer X, date").
  • Label ranges as starting points. Don't present your printer's tuned value as universal.
  • Add photos of failures and fixes to docs/assets/img/ (JPG/WebP, ≤ 300 KB, your own photos only).
  • Add tags in the page front matter (material, printer, problem type) so search and the tag index pick it up.
  • One topic per PR is easiest to review.
  • Use the page template for new pages.

docs.title: Design for printing
docs.text: Rules of thumb for parts you model yourself. All values are starting points for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Print a tolerance test on your own printer and adjust. Reference: Prusa KB: Modeling with 3D printing in mind.

docs.title: Tolerances & clearances
docs.text:
Fit Gap per side (typical start) Example Press / interference fit 0.0–0.1 mm Pins meant to stay put Snug / slip fit 0.15–0.2 mm Lids, sliding parts Loose / free fit 0.3–0.4 mm Hinges and print-in-place moving parts Print-in-place gaps ≥ 0.3–0.5 mm Articulated toys, captive joints

Account for material shrink (ABS/PA more than PLA) and elephant's foot on mating bottom edges (add a 0.3–0.5 mm chamfer).

docs.title: Holes
docs.text:
• Vertical holes print undersized, often by 0.1–0.3 mm. Add clearance, use slicer hole compensation (X-Y hole compensation), or drill or ream to final size.
  • Horizontal holes: make the top a teardrop or diamond so it's self-supporting, or use support. Otherwise the top sags.
  • For accurate bearing or shaft fits, print slightly undersize and ream.

docs.title: Orientation for strength
docs.text:
• Layers are the weak direction. Loads should run along the layers, not pull them apart. A hook printed upright snaps at a layer line. Printed lying flat, it doesn't.
  • Overhangs up to ~45° usually print without support. Bridges up to ~10–20 mm depending on material and cooling.
  • Put cosmetic faces up or on the side, not on supports. Add a flat base or split the model if it can't sit flat.

docs.title: Walls vs infill
docs.text:
• Walls (perimeters) carry most of the load for bending and torsion. Going from 2 to 4 walls often helps more than doubling infill.
  • Typical functional starting point: 3–4 walls, 4–5 top/bottom layers, 15–30 % gyroid or cubic infill.
  • Around bolt holes and inserts, add wall thickness locally (modifiers) rather than raising global infill.
  • More infill ≠ proportionally more strength, and it costs time, weight, and filament. (Also covered in my Build stronger prints guide.)
  • Myths to avoid: see Ellis: Misconceptions & bad advice.

docs.title: Threads, inserts & fasteners
docs.text: Method Best for Design notes Heat-set inserts (brass) Repeated assembly, strong threads Hole per the insert maker's spec (usually slightly smaller than the insert OD, with a tapered lead-in). ≥ 3 walls around it. Install with a soldering iron about 10–20 °C above the filament's print temp. See Prusa: heat-set inserts & tools Self-tapping screws into plastic Quick, low-cycle joints Pilot hole ≈ 80–85 % of screw OD. Extra walls Captive nuts (hex pocket) Cheap, strong Hex pocket +0.2–0.3 mm across flats. Slot from the side or insert with a pause-at-layer Printed threads ≥ M8 / large threads Use a modeled thread with ~0.2–0.4 mm clearance. Print vertically. Small printed threads are weak

docs.title: Other tips
docs.text:
• Minimum wall ≈ 2 × nozzle width (0.8 mm for 0.4 mm nozzle). Minimum feature ≈ nozzle width.
  • Fillets at stress points. Chamfers on bottom edges (not fillets, which overhang).
  • Text: embossed ≥ 0.6 mm tall and ≥ 1 mm wide strokes print best on vertical faces.
  • Design multi-color parts as separate bodies (or 3MF parts) so the slicer can assign filaments.

docs.title: Support removal
docs.text:
• Use flush cutters, needle-nose pliers, and a deburring tool. Wear eye protection, since PLA shards fly.
  • Remove PA supports within ~2 hours of printing, before they absorb moisture (Bambu Wiki: Support).
  • Soluble interfaces: PVA/BVOH in warm water, HIPS in d-limonene.

docs.title: Sanding & filling
docs.text:
Prusa's step-by-step approach (Prusa blog: Postprocessing step by step):

  1. Rough sand (~P100–P200) to knock down layer lines and seams.
  2. Fill gaps with filler or filler primer. Repeat filler and sanding until smooth.
  3. Finish with ~P400+, wet sanding for PLA so heat and friction don't melt and clog the paper.
  4. Prime → paint → clear coat.

docs.title: Chemical smoothing
docs.text:
• ABS and ASA smooth with acetone vapor for a glossy, molded look, but sharp details soften and thin parts can deform. (Prusa blog: Chemical smoothing)
  • PLA and PETG don't smooth with acetone.
  • Solvents are flammable and their vapors are hazardous. Work outdoors or under extraction, away from ignition sources. See Safety.

docs.title: Other finishes
docs.text:
• Heat-set inserts: see Design → Threads & inserts.
  • Annealing (PLA, PA): can raise heat resistance and strength but causes shrinkage and warping. Test on a sample and scale the model to compensate.
  • Epoxy coating: fills layer lines and adds gloss and strength on decorative parts.
  • Heat gun: quickly removes stringing hairs and restores color in stress-whitened PLA. Pass briefly, don't linger.
  • Gluing: CA (super glue) for PLA/PETG/ABS. Acetone weld for ABS/ASA. Use a plastic-rated epoxy for mixed materials.

docs.title: Fix: troubleshooting by symptom
docs.text:
Find the symptom, check the causes in order (most likely and cheapest first), and change one thing at a time.

First three questions for any failure

  1. Is the filament dry? (drying)
  2. Is the plate clean and correct for this material?
  3. Is the profile for this exact filament, nozzle, and printer?

Difficulty is easy (clean, dry, or one slider), medium (a test plus a mechanical check), or hard (the printer's mechanics). The same records are in data/troubleshooting.json.

Defect What you see Difficulty Start here Stringing Fine hairs or threads between separate parts of the print. easy Dry the spool, then print again before you change retraction. Warping Corners lift, or the base curls up off the plate. medium Close the enclosure, preheat the chamber, and keep drafts and air conditioning off the printer. Layer shift Layers step sideways, like a staircase, partway up the print. medium Fix the warp or the curl. Turn on Z-hop. Cool overhangs more on PLA and PETG. Elephant's foot The first layers bulge wider than the rest of the part. easy Raise Z-offset a little, or run bed leveling again. Under-extrusion Gaps, thin walls, or missing lines. The part looks starved of plastic. medium Slow down, or set a max volumetric speed from a calibration print. Z-banding Regular horizontal ridges repeating up the walls. hard Clean the screws, check the coupler, and make sure Z moves freely. Lubricate only where the maker says to. Bed adhesion The first layer will not stick, or the part pops off mid-print. easy Wash PEI with dish soap and hot water. Wipe with isopropyl alcohol between prints. Wet filament Popping or hissing at the nozzle, a rough or fuzzy surface, or sudden stringing on a profile that used to work. easy Dry it at the temperature and time on the material page, then store it sealed with desiccant. Spaghetti A loose nest of filament, usually because the part detached or a layer printed in the air. easy Stop the print. Fix adhesion: clean plate, Z-offset, brim, and no drafts. Nozzle clog The extruder clicks, plastic stops coming out, or the print turns hollow partway up. medium Heat the nozzle and do a cold pull using your printer's temperatures, or swap the nozzle.

docs.title: Stringing
docs.text:
Difficulty: easy. Dry the spool before you touch retraction.

Likely cause Fix Wet filament (very common with PETG, TPU, PA) Dry it (table), then re-test before touching settings Nozzle too hot Drop 5–10 °C, or run a temp tower Retraction too short or slow Run a retraction test. Direct drive is usually ~0.4–1.5 mm Long travel over open air Enable avoid crossing walls / combing. Arrange parts closer together Pressure advance off Calibrate PA / Flow Dynamics

Source: Prusa KB: Stringing and oozing

docs.title: Warping
docs.text:
Difficulty: medium. Drafts and an open door matter as much as the slicer.

Likely cause Fix Large temperature difference between part and room (ABS, ASA, PC, PA) Enclosure closed, chamber pre-heated, no drafts or AC nearby Too much part cooling Reduce or turn off the fan for ABS/ASA/PC. Use 10–20 % only for overhangs Weak first-layer grip Clean the plate (IPA or soap), use glue stick, check first-layer squish Sharp corners, large footprint Add a brim or mouse ears. Use a draft shield. Round corners in CAD Printing too fast Slow the first layers and outer walls

Source: Prusa KB: Warping · Prusa KB: Enclosure guidepost

docs.title: Layer shifts
docs.text:
Difficulty: medium. Listen for a thud. That is a skipped step, not a bad model.

Likely cause Fix Nozzle collided with a curled-up part Fix warping/curling. Enable Z-hop. Increase cooling on overhangs (PLA/PETG) Belt tension off or a loose pulley grub screw Check belt tension per the maker. Tighten pulley grub screws (one on the shaft flat) Obstruction (cable, filament scrap, spool tangle) Clear the path. Check the spool feeds freely Accelerations too high for the machine or load Lower acceleration/speed. Re-run input shaping if the printer has it Motor or driver overheating Check ventilation around electronics

Source: Prusa KB: Layer shifting · Ellis: Layer shifting

docs.title: Elephant's foot
docs.text:
Difficulty: easy. The bottom is squished or still soft.

Likely cause Fix First layer squished too much (nozzle too low) Raise Z-offset slightly or re-run bed leveling Bed too hot, so the bottom layers sag Lower the bed 5–10 °C after the first layer Heavy part on soft bottom layers Use the slicer's elephant foot compensation (~0.1–0.2 mm), or chamfer bottom edges in CAD (0.5 mm × 45°)

Source: Prusa KB: Elephant foot compensation

docs.title: Under-extrusion
docs.text:
Difficulty: medium. Not enough plastic is leaving the nozzle.

Likely cause Fix Printing faster than the hotend can melt Lower speed, or set max volumetric speed from calibration Partial clog / worn nozzle Cold pull or replace the nozzle. CF/GF fills wear brass nozzles quickly Nozzle too close on the first layer Re-level / adjust Z-offset Dirty or misaligned extruder gears, wrong idler tension Clean gears, check tension Heat creep (PLA in a hot enclosure) Open the lid/door for PLA. Check the hotend fan Wet or out-of-spec filament, tangled spool, AMS/CFS feed drag Dry it, check the spool path and buffer Wrong flow ratio Run the flow test

Source: Prusa KB: Under-extrusion

docs.title: Z-banding
docs.text:
Difficulty: hard. Regular ridges are usually the Z axis, not the filament profile.

Regular, repeating horizontal ridges (often matching the lead screw pitch) are usually mechanical. Irregular ridges are usually extrusion or temperature problems.

Likely cause Fix Lead screw / Z-coupler misaligned, binding, or dirty Clean the screws. Check the coupler and that the Z axis moves freely. Lubricate only where the maker's maintenance guide says to Layer height not a multiple of the Z motor's full step Use "magic numbers" (e.g. 0.04 mm multiples on many 8 mm-lead machines) Bed or hotend temperature oscillating Run PID tuning / check thermistor seating Inconsistent filament diameter, or wet filament Try a known-good spool Wobbly frame / loose gantry Check frame screws and eccentric nuts/rollers

Source: Prusa KB: Regular printer maintenance (MK4/MK3.9) (lead-screw care). Banding causes are general community knowledge, verify for your printer.

docs.title: Bed adhesion
docs.text:
Difficulty: easy. Clean plate, correct Z-offset, then temperature.

Likely cause Fix Fingerprints or oil on the plate Wash with dish soap and hot water (PEI). Wipe with IPA between prints Z-offset too high (no squish) Lower slightly. Lines should be flattened and touching, not transparent Wrong plate or release agent for the material PETG on smooth PEI → glue as a release layer. ABS/ASA/PC/PA → glue stick Bed temperature off Use the matrix range. Too hot can also hurt (PLA sagging) Drafts / cold room Close the enclosure. Avoid fans and AC Tiny contact area Add a brim. Re-orient the part

Source: Prusa KB: First layer issues · Ellis: Build surface adhesion

docs.title: Wet filament
docs.text:
Difficulty: easy. If it pops at the nozzle, dry it before you retune the profile.

Symptom Fix Popping or hissing at the nozzle, steam Dry it (temps & times) Bubbles, rough or fuzzy surface, loss of gloss Dry it, then store it sealed with desiccant Sudden stringing on a profile that used to be fine Dry before re-tuning retraction Weak layers, brittle filament that snaps Dry it. If it's still brittle, the spool may be degraded Supports on PA fused or hard to remove Remove supports within ~2 h of printing (Bambu)

Source: Prusa KB: Drying filament · Bambu Wiki: Filament drying

docs.title: Spaghetti
docs.text:
Difficulty: easy. A nest of loose filament means the part let go, or a layer printed in the air.

Stop the job. Do not peel hot plastic off the nozzle with your fingers. Clear the cooled blob, then fix bed adhesion and watch the next first layer. If the printer has a camera failure check, turn it on for long prints.

docs.title: Nozzle clog
docs.text:
Difficulty: medium. The extruder clicks and the print goes hollow.

Heat the nozzle and try a cold pull at the temperatures in your printer's guide, or fit a fresh nozzle. On PLA, open the enclosure so heat creep does not soften the filament above the melt zone. If you print carbon fiber, the nozzle should be hardened, not plain brass. The same causes are listed under under-extrusion.

Add your failure

Got a good photo of one of these? Save it as docs/assets/img/fix-<symptom>.jpg, update the image link above, and open a PR. See Contribute. My private failure log is a good source of these photos.

docs.title: Fleet comparison
docs.text:
Six printers: Bambu X1C, Bambu X2D, Creality Hi, Creality K2 Plus, Snapmaker U1, Flashforge Creator 5 Pro. Inventory notes: one K2 Plus with two CFS units; the X1C has a Panda Breath chamber heater, two "AMS Pro" units and one AMS.

Read these caveats before trusting a number

  • Maximum temperatures are limits, not recommended settings. Use the material matrix and the filament label.
  • Suggested uses are practical judgments based on the hardware, not benchmark rankings.
  • Tool changers avoid repeatedly unloading one nozzle, but they can still need priming or a prime tower. AMS/CFS switching usually needs purge material.
  • Material compatibility depends on the specific filament, nozzle, drying, enclosure, and profile.
  • No automatic transfer of the retired P1S's AMS to the Hi is assumed.

To verify before publishing: "AMS Pro" naming

"AMS Pro" is my own label for those units. Bambu Lab's current wiki names its units AMS, AMS 2 Pro, AMS HT, and AMS lite (see Bambu Lab Wiki: Filament Drying Recommendations, checked 2026-10-31). Check the model label on each unit and change "AMS Pro" to the official name (probably AMS 2 Pro) before sharing. The same page says AMS 2 Pro units on an X1 need their own power adapter for drying, while the X2D can power one from the printer.

docs.title: Maintain: maintenance checklist
docs.text: A generic schedule. The manufacturer's maintenance page for your printer wins where it differs. Bambu: X1 Maintenance Recommendation. Prusa (a clear general reference): Regular printer maintenance.

docs.title: Calendar
docs.text:
When The idea Do the section below Every print The plate and the nozzle tell you the truth Every print / daily Weekly, or about 50 print hours Dust and filament crumbs Weekly Monthly, or about 200 print hours Belts, gears, fans Monthly A few times a year Parts that wear out slowly Every 3–6 months Once a year A quiet hour with the power off Yearly

Hours are a nudge, not a service manual. A printer that runs all day hits "monthly" in a week. A printer that runs on Sundays can stay on the calendar.

docs.title: Every print / daily
docs.text:
• Clean the plate (IPA wipe, soap and water for PEI when grip drops)
  • Clear purge waste, poop chute, and wiper
  • Check the nozzle for blobs or wrap. Watch the first layer

docs.title: Weekly (or ~50 print hours)
docs.text:
• Brush or wipe the nozzle and silicone sock. Check the sock for tears
  • Clean dust and filament bits from rails, rods, and the bed area
  • Check AMS/CFS/feeder paths for filament dust and shavings. Look at PTFE tube ends for wear
  • Check desiccant in AMS/CFS units and dry boxes

docs.title: Monthly (or ~200 hours)
docs.text:
• Lubricate rods/rails/lead screws only as specified for that printer
  • Check belt tension and pulley grub screws
  • Clean extruder gears. Check the cutter (AMS/CFS) and filament sensors
  • Clean fans (hotend, part cooling, chamber) and check the chamber/carbon filter
  • Tool changers (U1, Creator 5 Pro): clean docks and wipers. Re-run tool-offset calibration

docs.title: Yearly
docs.text:
• Power off and look at the frame: loose screws, cracked printed parts, worn cable chains
  • Update firmware only from the maker, and read the note before you confirm
  • Run a full calibration (bed mesh, input shaping, flow) and save it
  • Replace the nozzle if the tip looks oval, even if fiber filament is not the reason
  • Order the spare you used up this year so the next failure is a ten-minute job

docs.title: Every 3–6 months / as needed
docs.text:
• Replace the nozzle (sooner with CF/GF in brass or stainless)
  • Replace carbon/HEPA filters per the maker
  • Re-run full calibration (bed mesh, input shaping, flow dynamics)
  • Check wiring and cable chains for wear. Tighten frame screws
  • Cold pull if extrusion degrades. See e.g. Prusa KB: Cold pull (method varies by hotend, so check your printer's guide)

docs.title: Spares worth keeping on hand
docs.text:
Nozzles (including hardened), silicone socks, PTFE tube, wiper/brush, AMS/CFS cutter blade, build plate, thermal paste or hotend kit, belts, desiccant, glue stick, IPA.

Per-printer logs

My dashboard's private Maintenance tracker holds due dates and history. Friends: copy this checklist into whatever you use.

docs.title: Material matrix
docs.text:
Starting points, not settings

These are typical, widely used ranges for standard grades, cross-checked against the Prusa Material Guide and Bambu Lab Filament Guide. The temperature printed on your spool and your printer's own filament profile come first. Specialty blends (silk, high-flow, CF/GF, "HF", "Pro") can be well outside these ranges. Check each against the fleet's max temps.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Material Nozzle °C Bed °C Chamber Dry (°C / h) Enclosure Common failures PLA 190–230 45–65 Keep it cool: lid/door open, ideally < ~35 °C 45–55 / 4–8 No (cooling matters more) Heat creep and clogs in a hot enclosure, stringing, soft overhangs if under-cooled PETG 220–260 70–90 Ambient 55–65 / 4–8 No Stringing and blobs, over-sticking to smooth PEI (glue or release agent), wet-filament bubbles ABS / ASA 240–270 90–110 Warm, ~40–60 °C passive or heated 60–80 / 4–8 Yes Warping/lifted corners, layer splitting on tall parts, fumes (styrene) TPU (95A typical) 210–240 30–60 Ambient 50–60 / 4–8 No Buckling in the extruder, stringing, feeder/AMS incompatibility, slow print speeds required PA / PA-CF 260–300 80–110 Warm–hot, ~40–60 °C+ 70–90 / 8–12 Yes Very hygroscopic (dry before every print), warping, stringing, abrasive CF wears soft nozzles PC (and PC blends) 260–300 100–120 Hot, ~50–60 °C+ 70–90 / 6–8 Yes Severe warping, layer cracking, adhesion loss without glue/brim

Chamber values are typical targets for enclosed printers. Active chamber heating on my fleet: K2 Plus up to 60 °C; X2D and Creator 5 Pro up to 65 °C; X1C via the aftermarket Panda Breath (not verified).

docs.title: Per-material notes
docs.text:
PLAPETGABS / ASATPUPA / PA-CFPC
  • Easiest material. Needs strong part cooling. Print with the lid open or door ajar on enclosed machines.
  • Specialty PLAs: silk prints slower and hotter, wood/glow/CF fills are abrasive or clog-prone, so use 0.4 mm hardened or larger nozzles.
  • Softens around 55–60 °C, so it's not for car interiors or hot rooms.
  • Source: Prusa KB: PLA
  • Tougher and more heat-tolerant than PLA. Moderate cooling.
  • Bonds very strongly to smooth PEI, so use glue stick or a textured plate as a release layer.
  • Stringing is usually wet filament or too-high temperature. Dry it before you change retraction.
  • PETG and PLA barely bond to each other, which makes them a classic support-interface pair (see Multi-material).
  • Source: Prusa KB: PETG
  • Needs an enclosure, low or no part cooling, glue, and a brim on large footprints.
  • ASA is UV-stable for outdoor parts; ABS is cheaper and easy to acetone-smooth (so is ASA).
  • Ventilate: both emit styrene. See Safety.
  • Sources: Prusa KB: ABS · Prusa KB: ASA
  • Print slowly (low volumetric flow), with minimal retraction.
  • Check that your exact TPU grade is approved for your AMS/CFS/feeder. Softer grades usually aren't. Use an external spool when in doubt.
  • Shore A and Shore D are different scales, so compare the maker's data sheet rather than a chart.
  • Source: Prusa KB: Flexible materials
  • Strong, tough, heat-resistant, and extremely moisture-sensitive. Print straight from a dryer or dry box.
  • CF/GF fills are abrasive. Use a hardened steel nozzle and extruder gears rated for them.
  • Bambu notes that supports on PA should be removed within ~2 hours, before the part absorbs moisture (Bambu Wiki: Support).
  • Source: Prusa KB: Polyamide (Nylon)
  • Very high heat resistance and toughness. The hardest of these to keep flat.
  • Hot chamber, glue, a brim, slow first layers, and no drafts.
  • Source: Prusa KB: Polycarbonate

docs.title: Choosing by requirement
docs.text:
Need Try first Then Easy, detailed, indoor PLA PETG Outdoors / UV ASA PETG (short-term) Heat near engines, cars, lamps ASA, PC PA-CF Tough + slightly flexible (clips, hinges) PETG PA Rubbery grip, dampers TPU — Stiff, strong, engineering PA-CF PC

See also: Drying & storage · Material notes from my guides

docs.title: Materials 101
docs.text:
Start with PLA. It is stiff, it likes a cool breeze, and a failed print is cheap. Move to PETG when you want something tougher. Try TPU when you want it bendy. Leave ABS and ASA until you have an enclosure and a plan for the smell.

The ranges below are the same starting points as the material matrix, checked against Prusa's material articles and Bambu's filament guide. Type the number from your spool first. A silk PLA or a "high flow" PETG can sit outside the band.

Dry times are for a filament dryer or a warm oven you trust not to melt the spool. When in doubt, use the dryer's preset for that plastic.

Start hereLater Material Nozzle °C Bed °C Enclosure Dry Good for Watch out PLA 190–230 45–65 no 45–55 °C, 4–8 h First prints, models, and indoor parts that will not get hot. Softens around a hot car or a sunny windowsill. Strings if it is wet or too hot. PETG 220–260 70–90 optional 55–65 °C, 4–8 h Clips, brackets, and parts that need to be tougher than PLA. Strings. Sticks hard to smooth PEI, so use glue or a textured plate as a release layer. TPU 210–240 30–60 no 50–60 °C, 4–8 h Grips, bumpers, and hinges. 95A is a common firm grade. Print slowly. Soft grades buckle in the extruder and are often banned from AMS/CFS units. Check the spool. ABS 240–270 90–110 yes 60–80 °C, 4–8 h Functional parts that see more heat than PLA, when you can enclose and ventilate. Warps. Gives off styrene. Do not print it in a bedroom. See Safety. ASA 240–270 90–110 yes 60–80 °C, 4–8 h Outdoor parts. It handles sunlight better than ABS. Warps like ABS and needs the same ventilation. Acetone smoothing works, outdoors. Material Nozzle °C Bed °C Enclosure Dry Good for Watch out PA / nylon 260–300 80–110 yes 70–90 °C, 8–12 h Strong, tough parts that see heat and impact. Extremely hygroscopic. Dry it before every print and keep it in a dry box. Carbon fiber wears brass nozzles. PC 260–300 100–120 yes 70–90 °C, 6–8 h Parts that must stay stiff when hot. Warps badly. Use glue, a brim, slow first layers, and no drafts.

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
You need Buy A first spool, a model, a clip that lives indoors PLA A bracket that gets bumped, or a bit more heat than PLA PETG A grip, a foot, a hinge TPU, and check that your filament changer allows that softness A part in the sun ASA, enclosed, ventilated A part near heat, once the easy plastics are boring The "Later" tab: nylon or PC, dry, enclosed

PLA and PETG barely stick to each other. That is annoying in a part and useful when one of them is only support. See multi-material planning.

More temperatures, drying, and failure notes: material matrix and drying and storage.

docs.title: Filament drying & storage
docs.text: Most FDM filaments are hygroscopic: they absorb moisture from the air. Wet filament shows up as stringing, popping or hissing at the nozzle, bubbles, rough or fuzzy surfaces, and weak layers. Dry before you re-tune.

docs.title: Drying starting points
docs.text:
Material Temp (°C) Time (h) Prusa reference (Prusament) How sensitive PLA 45–55 4–8 45 °C / 6 h Low–moderate PETG 55–65 4–8 55 °C / 6 h Moderate ABS 60–80 4–6 — Moderate ASA 70–80 4–6 80 °C / 4 h Moderate TPU 50–60 4–8 60 °C / 4–6 h High PA / PA-CF 70–90 8–12 PA11-CF: 90 °C / 6 h Very high PC / PC blend 70–90 6–8 PC Blend: 85 °C / 5 h High PVA / BVOH (supports) 45–55 8+ — Very high

Sources: Prusa KB: Drying filament · Bambu Lab Wiki: Filament Drying Recommendations. Always check the filament maker's data sheet. Don't exceed the spool's rated temperature. Many cardboard and cheap plastic spools deform above ~60–70 °C.

What my gear can do (verify against current docs)

  • Bambu AMS 2 Pro / AMS HT can dry in place. Bambu notes that AMS 2 Pro tops out around 65 °C, so it may not fully dry high-temp materials, and that AMS HT handles all filaments. Static drying mode isn't suitable for PLA, PVA, Support for PLA/PETG, or TPU (spools can stick). On an X1, each AMS 2 Pro needs its own power adapter to dry. The X2D can power one from the printer. (Bambu Wiki)
  • Bambu also documents heated-bed drying on enclosed X-series printers, with the filament covered on the bed.
  • Creality CFS / Snapmaker U1 / Creator 5 Pro: add your dryer or dry-box notes here (PRs welcome).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Target < 20 % RH in storage for sensitive materials (PA, PC, TPU, PVA). Keep everything else below ~30–40 %.
  • Airtight boxes or vacuum bags with silica gel desiccant plus a cheap hygrometer. Recharge the desiccant when it changes color.
  • Return spools to storage right after printing. Print PA and PVA straight from a dry box.
  • Label each spool with its open/dry date.

docs.title: Is it wet? Quick checks
docs.text:
1. Listen for crackling or popping at the nozzle during a purge or extrusion.
  2. Look for steam, bubbles, or a rough, matte, fuzzy surface where it should be glossy.
  3. Watch for a sudden increase in stringing on a profile that used to be clean.
  4. Snap test (PLA/PETG): wet filament often becomes brittle and snaps when bent.

See also: Fix → Wet filament

docs.title: Material notes (from my saved guides)
docs.text:
Source & status

Summaries of instructional visuals I saved from AD3D (@ad3duae), added October 25, 2026. These are my summaries, not the original images, and the numbers inside the visuals have not been independently validated. Use the filament and printer maker's guidance for temperatures, drying, compatibility, and safety. See Credits & licensing.

docs.title: ASA printing guide
docs.text:
• Check drying requirements and store sealed with desiccant.
  • Use the filament maker's ASA profile and confirm the printer, plate, and nozzle suit it.
  • Enclosure, glue, and a brim when needed to reduce warping.
  • Run a small test print and check adhesion and layer bonding before a long job.
  • Ventilate (see Safety).

docs.title: ABS printing guide
docs.text:
• Check dryness and use the maker's ABS profile. Confirm the enclosure and plate are suitable.
  • Keep temperatures stable, part cooling low, and use glue and a brim when needed.
  • Check a test print for lifted corners and layer cracking before scaling up.

docs.title: PLA printing guide
docs.text:
• Choose the exact PLA type in the slicer. Silk, wood, CF, glow, and aero PLA all differ.
  • Filled or abrasive types (glow, CF) may need a hardened nozzle.
  • Use a small test to check flow, surface, and cooling.

docs.title: PETG printing guide
docs.text:
• Check dryness before changing several slicer settings.
  • Start from the profile for your exact PETG product (is it a high-flow variant?).
  • Change one variable at a time. The visual's 220 °C and flow values are source-specific suggestions, not universal settings.

docs.title: TPU essentials & TPU types
docs.text:
• Confirm the TPU grade, nozzle, and feed path. Don't assume AMS compatibility from "TPU" alone.
  • The source's Bambu workflow suggests disabling Flow Dynamics Calibration for TPU and using PLA as the support where the printer supports that combination.
  • Choose hardness by the job: cushioning and grip (soft), moderate flex, or rigidity and wear resistance (hard). Shore A ≠ Shore D. Conversion charts are approximate.

docs.title: OBJ vs. STL in Bambu Studio
docs.text:
• STL = mesh geometry. OBJ can reference colors and materials via its MTL file. Keep OBJ, MTL, and textures together.
  • Drag the OBJ into Bambu Studio, review the color-matching dialog, assign filaments, and inspect the slice.

docs.title: Build stronger prints
docs.text:
• Orient the part so the load doesn't pull layers apart.
  • Walls before infill. More infill doesn't give proportionally more strength.
  • Pick infill pattern and density for the actual use, and test the finished part under its real load.
  • More in Design for printing.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
Everything between "I have a model" and "press print":

  • Slicer basics: the ten settings that matter if you are new.
  • Calibration sequence: tune each new filament on each printer once, then save the profile.
  • Slicer tips: seam placement, support tuning, and strength settings.
  • Multi-material planning: tool changer vs AMS/CFS, purge, and support-interface pairs.

Pre-flight checklist

  • Right printer for size, material, and colors (selector)
  • Filament dry (drying); right nozzle (hardened for CF/GF)
  • Profile matches the exact filament and nozzle
  • Plate clean (IPA, or dish soap and water for PEI) with the right release agent or glue
  • Preview checked: seams, supports, first layer, travel
  • Enclosure lid/door set correctly for the material (open for PLA, closed for ABS/ASA/PC/PA)

docs.title: Calibration sequence
docs.text:
Calibrate per printer × per filament × per nozzle. Save the result as a named filament profile, such as PETG-Brand-X1C-0.4.

Order matters

The OrcaSlicer Calibration Guide recommends temperature → max volumetric speed → pressure advance → flow ratio → retraction, because each step depends on the one before. Shrinkage/tolerance comes last. Bambu printers with auto-calibration (X1C/X2D Flow Dynamics) can cover PA automatically. Run the manual tests when the auto result looks wrong.

# Test What you're finding How to read it Reference 1 Temperature tower Best nozzle temp for this spool Pick the block with the best balance of layer bonding, bridges/overhangs, surface, and stringing. Lean higher for fast or high-flow printing Orca: Temp calibration 2 Max volumetric speed Flow ceiling before under-extrusion Note where gaps or rough walls start, then set ~10–20 % below that Orca: Max volumetric speed 3 Pressure advance (Bambu: Flow Dynamics) Corner sharpness and even lines at speed changes Choose the line or corner with no bulge or gap at speed transitions Orca: Pressure advance · Bambu Wiki: Flow Dynamics · Ellis: PA/LA 4 Flow ratio (extrusion multiplier) Correct amount of plastic Smoothest top surface without ridges (over) or gaps (under) Orca: Flow ratio · Bambu Wiki: Flow rate · Ellis: Extrusion multiplier 5 Retraction Shortest retraction with clean travel Lowest section without strings. Direct drive is usually ~0.4–1.5 mm. Dry the filament first Orca: Retraction test 6 Shrinkage / tolerance Dimensional accuracy and fit Print a 50–100 mm XY test and measure with calipers. Set the filament's shrinkage %. Use a tolerance test for peg/hole fits Orca: Tolerance test

Shrinkage quick math

shrinkage % = measured ÷ designed × 100. A 100 mm design that measures 99.4 mm gives 99.4 %. PLA/PETG are usually 99.6–100 %. ABS/ASA/PC/PA typically shrink more. Measure, don't guess.

docs.title: My results
docs.text:
Fill in as you go. PRs from friends with their own results are welcome (add your printer name).

Printer Filament (brand / type) Nozzle Temp °C Max vol. speed mm³/s PA / K Flow ratio Retraction mm Shrinkage % Date X1C e.g. PLA Basic 0.4 hardened auto X2D K2 Plus Hi U1 (T0–T3) Creator 5 Pro (T0–T3)

Tool changers

On the U1 and Creator 5 Pro, each toolhead is its own hotend, so check per-tool XY offsets (the printer's own tool-alignment calibration) and calibrate flow/PA per tool if results differ.

docs.title: Multi-material planning
docs.text: My fleet has three different approaches: single nozzle + switcher (X1C + AMS, K2 Plus + CFS, Hi + optional CFS), dual nozzle (X2D), and independent tool changers (Snapmaker U1, Creator 5 Pro). Choosing the right one saves a lot of waste and time.

docs.title: Tool changer vs AMS/CFS
docs.text:
Tool changer (U1, Creator 5 Pro) Dual nozzle (X2D) Single nozzle + AMS/CFS (X1C, K2 Plus, Hi) Materials per job 4 (one per tool) 2 hotends, with AMS feeding them Up to 16 slots (more units) Waste per swap Small: prime/wipe only Small between nozzles; purge within one nozzle's slots Full purge of the previous color each swap Time per swap Seconds (tool park/pick) Fast between nozzles Slow: cut, retract, load, purge Mixed materials (PLA + PETG, PLA + TPU) Excellent, each tool tuned separately Good: body on one nozzle, support/interface on the other Possible, but each swap purges and temps change Best for 2–4 colors with many swaps per layer, support interfaces, mixed materials Support-heavy parts with a dedicated interface material Many colors with few swaps (e.g. color-by-height, signs)

Rules of thumb

  • Swaps per layer × layers = waste. A 4-color model with color changes on every layer belongs on a tool changer.
  • Few colors that change by height (stacked bands) → AMS/CFS is fine.
  • Want a support-interface material? → X2D, U1, or Creator 5 Pro first.

docs.title: Purge & prime
docs.text:
• Flushing volume (single-nozzle) depends on the color pair. Dark → light needs the most. Bambu Studio sets it per from/to pair, with a multiplier. Lower it carefully and test for color bleed. (Bambu Wiki: Reduce waste during filament change)
  • Prime tower stabilizes pressure after a swap. Tool changers can still need one. (Bambu Wiki: Prime tower)
  • Waste reducers: flush into infill / flush into objects, group color changes, order filaments light → dark, print several copies per plate so one tower serves them all.

docs.title: Support-interface pairs
docs.text:
The idea: a material that doesn't bond well to the body is used only for the interface layers, so supports pop off cleanly with a smooth underside. Then top Z distance can be 0 (Bambu Wiki: Support).

Body material Interface material Notes PLA PETG Classic pair: they barely bond. Cheap and easy PETG PLA Works the other way too PLA Bambu Support for PLA (Support W) / Support for PLA/PETG Purpose-made breakaway PLA / PETG PVA or BVOH Water-soluble for internal cavities. Very moisture-sensitive, keep dry ABS / ASA HIPS HIPS dissolves in d-limonene. Also breakaway PA / PA-CF / PET-CF Bambu Support for PA/PET Remove promptly. It absorbs moisture TPU PLA Suggested in my TPU guide where the printer supports the combo

Interface-only saves material

Print the support base in the body material and only the interface layers in the special material. That's fewer swaps and less purge (or no purge on a tool changer).

Verify per printer

Material pairing and temperatures must be in range for both tools/nozzles. Use each maker's guidance (the X2D listing says "use manufacturer guidance for support pairing").

docs.title: Slicer basics
docs.text:
A slicer cuts the model into layers and writes the file your printer runs. You can ignore most of the menus. These ten settings are the ones that change the result. Leave the rest on the printer's default profile until one of these is not enough.

Use the profile for your printer and your nozzle. A 0.4 mm nozzle is the usual one in the box. The deeper notes on seams and supports are Slicer tips. Tuning a new spool is the calibration sequence.

docs.title: 1. Layer height
docs.text: How thick each slice is. 0.20 mm is a normal everyday height on a 0.4 mm nozzle. 0.12–0.16 mm looks smoother and takes longer. 0.28 mm is a draft. Stay under about 75% of the nozzle width so the lines still squash together. The printer profile already knows a safe list. Pick from that list.

docs.title: 2. Walls (perimeters)
docs.text: The solid outlines. Two walls is a display model. Three or four walls is the first thing to add when a part snaps. Walls do more for strength than stuffing the inside with infill.

docs.title: 3. Infill
docs.text: The lattice inside. 10–15% gyroid or grid is enough for most models and stands. 20–40% is for parts you will stand on or bolt down, and only after you have added walls. 100% infill is rarely the right answer. It is slow, and the part can still split between layers.

docs.title: 4. Nozzle and bed temperature
docs.text: Use the spool label, then the slicer's generic preset for that plastic if the label gives a range. Materials 101 has the usual bands. Change temperature in 5 °C steps. Hotter sticks layers together and strings more. Cooler looks cleaner and can go brittle.

docs.title: 5. Speed, really volumetric flow
docs.text: The big "500 mm/s" number is a maximum, not a promise. The hotend can only melt so much plastic per second. If walls look thin at high speed, you are past that limit. Slow the outer wall for looks. Leave the infill faster. The calibration page shows how to find a volumetric limit instead of guessing.

docs.title: 6. Part cooling
docs.text: The fan on the side of the nozzle. PLA wants it on, or bridges sag. ABS, ASA, and PC want it off or nearly off, or the part splits and lifts. PETG is in between. The material preset usually sets this. Do not "improve" it on the first print.

docs.title: 7. Supports
docs.text: Plastic scaffolding under overhangs. Turn them on when a slope is steeper than about 45 degrees from vertical, or when a bridge is long. Paint them on just the spots that need them if the slicer allows it. They scar the surface. A second material that does not bond (PLA supporting PETG, or a dedicated support filament) lets you set the gap to zero. Same-plastic supports need a gap or they become part of the model. Details: Slicer tips.

docs.title: 8. Brim, skirt, raft
docs.text: A skirt is a throwaway loop that primes the nozzle. Leave it on. A brim is a lip stuck to the first layer so corners do not lift. Use it on small feet and on ABS. A raft is a whole disposable platform. Use it when nothing else will stick, not as a habit.

docs.title: 9. Retraction
docs.text: A short pull of filament before the nozzle jumps, so it does not draw a hair. The printer profile's number is the right start. If you still see strings, dry the filament before you chase retraction. Direct-drive machines often land around 0.4–1.5 mm. That range is a test window from the stringing notes, not a value to type in blindly.

docs.title: 10. Seam
docs.text:
Every layer has to start somewhere. That start leaves a mark. Hide it on a corner or on the back of the part. You cannot turn it off. How the modes differ: Slicer tips.

A ten-minute practice: import a 20 mm cube or a simple clip, select your printer and PLA, set 0.20 mm layers and 3 walls, leave everything else, slice, and look at the preview. If the first layer in the preview is a solid sheet and the travels are not a bird's nest, print it.

docs.title: Slicer tips
docs.text:
Source

Seam and support sections are organized from my saved AD3D (@ad3duae) guides, whose visuals cite the Bambu Lab Wiki. Settings were not independently verified. Cross-checked against Bambu Wiki: Seam settings, Bambu Wiki: Support, and Prusa KB: Seam position.

docs.title: Seam position
docs.text:
The seam is where each layer's perimeter starts and stops. You can move it, but you can't make it disappear.

Mode What it does When to use it Nearest Picks a nearby, less-visible spot (concave corners), avoiding overhangs. May move between layers Models with hidden corners. Check in preview Aligned Tries to line the seam up vertically across layers One consistent line is easier to hide or sand Back Puts the seam toward the back of the plate (Y+), whatever the model orientation Rotate the model so the hidden face points to the back Random Scatters seam points around the surface When scattered marks look better than a line (may leave small zits)

Workflow (Bambu Studio): Quality → Seam → pick a mode → use Seam Painting for exact placement on a hidden edge → on curved surfaces consider Scarf joint seam (profile-dependent) → slice, preview, and test small before a long job.

docs.title: Support tuning
docs.text:
Three controls balance underside finish against easy removal. There's no single universal profile.

Setting Lower / fewer Higher / more Top Z distance (vertical gap) Better underside, harder removal, more scarring risk Easier removal, rougher underside Top interface layers Faster, less material, pattern may show through Smoother, flatter underside. Removal may get easier or harder Top interface spacing Denser contact, smoother, harder removal Easier removal, rougher underside

Test one change at a time:

  1. Save a copy of your working profile and use a small supported test model.
  2. Rough underside → smaller top Z distance or tighter interface spacing. Too hard to remove → increase the gap or spacing.
  3. Change top Z distance one layer height at a time, since rounding can change the real gap, especially with tree supports or when Independent support layer height is off.
  4. Adjust interface spacing in 0.05–0.1 mm steps.
  5. Interface layers = 0 disables the interface. The source suggests this may help PLA-on-PLA removal. Treat it as a test, not a default.
  6. Record material, layer height, the three settings, underside appearance, and removal effort.

Dedicated support material changes the rules

Bambu's wiki: with a dedicated support/interface filament (e.g. Bambu Support for PLA), top Z distance can be 0. With the same filament as the body, use about 0.2 mm, or removal gets very hard. 3 interface layers gives a stable, flat platform. (Bambu Wiki: Support) See Multi-material planning for interface pairs.

docs.title: Strength settings (quick version)
docs.text:
• Walls (perimeters) add strength faster than infill. Try 3–4 walls before raising infill above ~25 %.
  • Orient so loads run along layers, not across them.
  • Hotter (within range) and slower = better layer bonding. More cooling = better overhangs but weaker bonds.
  • Full details: Design for printing.

docs.title: Safety: ventilation & VOCs
docs.text: FDM printers release ultrafine particles (UFPs) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) while printing. Research from UL's Chemical Insights found emissions vary by filament, printer, and temperature. Higher-temperature materials such as ABS and nylon generally emit more, and the measured VOCs include styrene (ABS/ASA), caprolactam (nylon), formaldehyde, and acetaldehyde. (UL Chemical Insights: 3D printing emissions)

docs.title: Practical rules
docs.text:
Situation Do this PLA / PETG, occasional Ventilated room. Don't sit next to the printer for hours ABS / ASA / PC / PA Enclosed printer with filtration (carbon + HEPA) or ducted exhaust. Don't print these in a bedroom or poorly ventilated space Opening the enclosure after a hot print Let the filter run a few minutes after the print ends, then open Long or frequent jobs Put printers in a separate, ventilated room. Consider an air-quality monitor (PM2.5 / VOC) Acetone smoothing, solvents, resin (future) Outdoors or under extraction. Nitrile gloves and eye protection. Keep away from ignition sources
  • Filters wear out. Replace carbon filters on the maker's schedule.
  • Don't create drafts across the print (warping) when ventilating. Exhaust the enclosure, not the build plate.

docs.title: Fire and electricity
docs.text:
A printer is a heater that moves. Treat it like a kettle you do not walk away from until you trust it.

  • Don't leave a printer running in an empty house until it has finished many boring prints without a fault. Use the camera and failure detection when the machine has them.
  • A smoke detector in the room, and an ABC or CO₂ extinguisher you can reach without stepping over the printer.
  • Thermal-runaway protection should stay enabled. It cuts the heater if the temperature does not rise. Check it again after any firmware change.
  • Keep the spool and loose filament off the heated bed. A scrap on a 100 °C plate is how a small fire starts.
  • Do not stack a printer on a carpet or inside a cupboard with no air. The power supply needs the ventilation the maker designed.

docs.title: Enclosure
docs.text:
Close the box for ABS, ASA, nylon, and PC. Open the door or lid for PLA if the chamber has no "keep it cool" mode. The point of the box is still air, not a hotter room around the whole printer.

If the machine has a carbon or HEPA filter, leave the fan running for a few minutes after a hot job, then open the door. Filters fill up. Replace them on the maker's schedule, not when they look dirty.

An enclosure is also a guard. A CoreXY head at the speeds in the printer table is not something to reach into.

docs.title: Kids and pets
docs.text:
• The nozzle is hot enough to burn after the fans have stopped. The bed stays hot too.
  • Moving belts and a tool changer will pinch fingers. The rule is: if it is printing, the door stays shut and hands stay out.
  • Pets will eat filament scraps and chew a dangling spool. Cut waste goes in a bin with a lid, not on the floor.
  • Resin, isopropyl alcohol, and acetone do not live on a low shelf. Filament printers are the ones this page is about. A resin vat is a separate setup with gloves.
  • Show a child the stopped printer, not the running one. The interesting part is the finished object.

Not medical or industrial-hygiene advice

This is a hobbyist summary. Follow your printer and filament makers' safety data sheets (SDS) and local regulations.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
You do not need a workshop. A desk, a spool of PLA, and one afternoon is enough for a first print.

Work through these six steps in order. Each one has a checklist. When a step points at another page, that page goes deeper. You can skip the deep page until you need it.

docs.title: 1. What 3D printing is
docs.text:
A filament printer (FDM, also called FFF) melts a plastic string and draws the object in thin layers. The picture on your screen is a hollow shell with a lattice inside, not a solid block, unless you ask for that.

Resin printers shine light through a screen into liquid resin. They make finer detail and they are a worse first machine: gloves, washing, and curing, plus fumes. This site is about filament printers. Resin gets one mention in the buying guide so you know it exists.

The words you will see immediately: nozzle, filament, slicer, build plate. The glossary has the rest.

  • I can say, in one sentence, that the printer stacks melted plastic.
  • I know this site's filament pages are the path, and resin is a different hobby.

docs.title: 2. Choose a first printer
docs.text:
Buy for the things you will actually print in the next month, not for a spec you might want in a year.

For almost everyone that means PLA on an open-frame machine, or a small enclosed machine if you already know you want ABS. Multicolor is fun and it is also a second thing to learn. You can add it later on many printers.

Read what to buy, then the printer table. Prices there are dated. A dash means the maker's page did not say.

  • I wrote down the largest part I want, in millimeters, and the materials (start with PLA).
  • I picked a printer whose build volume is bigger than that part.
  • I checked today's price on the maker's site. The table can be a week old.

docs.title: 3. Unbox, level, and get a first layer
docs.text:
Most new printers arrive mostly built. Budget an hour, not a weekend. Follow the maker's card, not a random video of a different model.

The only skill that matters today is the first layer. Lines should look like a flat ribbon, stuck to each other, not a round thread and not a transparent smear.

  • The printer is on a sturdy table, with space behind it for the bed or the door.
  • I ran the on-screen setup: update, load filament, auto-level if it has it.
  • I washed the build plate with dish soap and water before the first print. New plates ship with a film of oil.
  • I watched a one-layer square or the printer's built-in first-layer test and adjusted Z-offset until the lines joined.

If the plastic will not stick, use the bed adhesion checks before you change anything else.

docs.title: 4. Print the sample that came with the printer
docs.text:
The printer's own sample is sliced for that machine. Use it. A model from the internet adds slicer choices you have not practiced yet.

Use the PLA that came in the box, or a fresh dry spool. Load it the way the screen says. Start the print and stay for the first ten minutes.

  • Filament is seated, and the end is cut straight, not crushed.
  • The nozzle and bed reached the temperatures on the screen before it started moving.
  • I stayed through the first layer. It stuck.
  • I let the part cool a little, then flexed the plate to pop it off. I did not pry with a metal knife into a PEI sheet.

A failed sample is still useful. Match what you see to the troubleshooting index and change one thing.

docs.title: 5. The slicer in ten minutes
docs.text:
A slicer turns a model file into instructions. You only need ten settings to leave the sample behind. They are listed, in order, on Slicer basics.

Download the slicer your printer's maker recommends (Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, Creality Print, OrcaSlicer, or the one named in the manual). Pick the printer profile that matches your model, not a similar one.

  • The slicer has my exact printer and a 0.4 mm nozzle, unless I bought a different size.
  • I opened one small STL, used the default PLA profile, and looked at the preview.
  • I can point at the walls, the infill, and the first layer in that preview.

docs.title: 6. What to print next
docs.text:
Print things you will use, small enough to finish in an hour.

Good second prints: a drawer divider, a cable clip, a scraper handle, a simple vase with the "vase mode" or spiral setting if you want to see the nozzle work. Skip articulated dragons and multi-day statues until a one-hour part looks clean.

Where to get files, and what the license lets you do, is on model sources.

  • I downloaded one model with a stated license and saved the link and the designer.
  • I sliced it at 0.20 mm layers, with a brim if it has small feet.
  • I watched the first layer again.
  • I wrote down what I would change next time (temperature, speed, or orientation) instead of changing five settings at once.

When that part is in your hand, the rest of this site is a reference, not a course. Materials 101 is the next page the first time you buy a different spool. Maintenance is the page the first time the printer has a week of dust on it.
